sectionB.q: Mitochondria are called the 'Power house of the cell'. Explain it in three points.
a: Mitochondria are double-membrane-bound organelles where aerobic respiration takes place.
They release energy from food and convert much of it into ATP (adenosine triphosphate).
ATP supplies usable energy for many cellular activities, so mitochondria are called the powerhouse of the cell.

sectionB.q: Write the three differences between apoptosis and necrosis.
a: Apoptosis is programmed, controlled cell death; necrosis is uncontrolled cell death caused by injury or other harmful conditions.
Apoptosis normally does not damage surrounding tissue; necrosis can damage nearby cells and produce inflammation.
Apoptosis removes unwanted cells as part of normal regulation; necrosis generally results from external damage such as toxins, infection or injury.

sectionB.q: Define Biodiversity and explain the importance of it.
a: Biodiversity is the degree of variation within or among species in different regions of Earth.
It provides useful products such as food, fibre, oil, rubber, timber and medicines.
It helps maintain ecosystem stability, recycles nutrients and contributes to reducing pollution.

sectionB.q: What is cell theory? And state its postulates.
a: Cell theory is the fundamental biological principle that the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
All living organisms are composed of one or more cells.
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of organisms.
New cells arise from pre-existing cells through cell division.

sectionB.q: Define the following: (i) Heterotrophic nutrition (ii) Vitamins (iii) Biotechnology
a: Heterotrophic nutrition: obtaining nutrients from other organisms or organic sources because the organism cannot prepare its own food.
Vitamins: organic micronutrients required in small amounts for normal metabolism, health and development.
Biotechnology: application of biological knowledge and techniques, including manipulation of genes, to obtain useful products or desirable characteristics.

sectionB.q: Write any three effects of malnutrition in human.
a: Starvation can result from severe deficiency of calories and nutrients.
An unbalanced diet can contribute to cardiovascular/heart disease.
Malnutrition can cause constipation and may also increase the risk of infection or obesity depending on the nutritional imbalance.

sectionB.q: Define Karyokinesis and describe the main events of prophase mitosis.
a: Karyokinesis is the division of the nucleus during cell division.
During prophase, chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes.
The nucleolus and nuclear membrane disappear, while spindle fibres begin to form and chromosomes become attached to the spindle.

sectionB.q: State the important carbohydrates in the continuation of life processes in living organisms.
a: Carbohydrates are important organic compounds and a major source of energy for living organisms.
Glucose is an important simple carbohydrate and is used in cellular respiration to release energy.
Starch is an important storage carbohydrate in plants, while glycogen is a storage carbohydrate in animals.

sectionB.q: Explain the composition and importance of Plasma in blood.
a: Plasma is the fluid part of blood in which blood cells and other substances are suspended.
It contains water, proteins, salts, nutrients, hormones, gases and waste products.
Plasma transports nutrients, hormones, gases and wastes and helps maintain the internal environment of the body.

sectionB.q: Describe the relationship of Biology with any other three science branches.
a: Biophysics applies laws and techniques of physics to explain biological processes.
Biomathematics/Biometry uses mathematics to collect and analyze biological data.
Biochemistry combines biology and chemistry to study the molecules that form living organisms and cells.

sectionB.q: Draw neat and labelled diagram of a plant cell.
a: Draw the textbook-style plant cell and label: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, nucleolus, large central vacuole, chloroplasts, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi bodies and ribosomes.
The diagram should be large, neat and clearly labelled with straight label lines.

sectionB.q: State the causes of deforestation and its effects on biodiversity.
a: Major causes include agriculture, livestock breeding, mining, paper/timber extraction, urbanization and road construction.
Deforestation destroys habitats and causes loss of biodiversity.
It can also increase soil erosion, disturb ecosystems and reduce the ability of forests to absorb carbon dioxide and control pollution.

sectionC.q: Draw neat and labelled diagram of Human Alimentary canal.
a: Draw and label the continuous alimentary canal: mouth/oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus.
Also label the accessory organs shown with the digestive system: liver, gall bladder and pancreas.
Keep the diagram neat, proportional and clearly labelled.

sectionC.q: Define enzyme. Describe the characteristics of it.
a: An enzyme is a biological catalyst that speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed in the reaction.
Most enzymes are proteins and are highly specific for their substrates.
Enzymes have an active site where the substrate binds.
Their activity is affected by temperature, pH and substrate concentration.
They lower the activation energy of reactions and may require cofactors or be affected by activators and inhibitors.

sectionC.q: Define mitosis, write its different stages and explain any two of them.
a: Mitosis is cell division in which one parent cell produces two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell.
Its main stages are prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by cytokinesis.
Prophase: chromosomes condense, the nuclear membrane disappears and spindle fibres form.
Metaphase: chromosomes arrange at the equator of the cell.
Anaphase: sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
Telophase: chromosomes reach the poles and new nuclear membranes form.

sectionC.q: Describe simple permanent tissues in detail.
a: Simple permanent tissues are made mainly of one type of cell and perform specific functions.
Parenchyma consists of living, relatively thin-walled cells and commonly stores food and may carry out photosynthesis when chloroplasts are present.
Collenchyma consists of living cells with unevenly thickened walls and provides flexible support to growing parts.
Sclerenchyma consists of thick, lignified cells and provides strength and mechanical support.

sectionC.q: Describe pulmonary and systemic circulation of blood in the human heart and state their importance.
a: Pulmonary circulation carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle through the pulmonary artery to the lungs and returns oxygenated blood to the left atrium through pulmonary veins.
Systemic circulation carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle through the aorta to body tissues and returns deoxygenated blood to the right atrium through the venae cavae.
Together they ensure continuous delivery of oxygen and nutrients to tissues and removal of carbon dioxide and other wastes.

sectionC.q: Define respiration. Write aerobic and anaerobic respiration with chemical equations.
a: Respiration is the cellular process in which food molecules are broken down to release usable energy.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP).
Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen. In alcoholic fermentation: C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2 + energy.
Anaerobic respiration releases less energy than complete aerobic respiration.
